summary: Aseptic practice reduces the introduction and transfer of microorganisms during care.
body: Hand hygiene, appropriate protective equipment and maintenance of a sterile field serve different purposes. A suspected break in technique needs correction; an intact-looking surface alone does not establish sterility.
reflect: How do clean technique and sterile technique serve different situations?

summary: Recovery assessment follows airway, breathing, circulation, consciousness, comfort and the effects of the procedure.
body: Anesthesia, pain and reduced movement can affect ventilation and mobility. Gastrointestinal function and wound findings also evolve. New fever or other changes require assessment of possible causes rather than automatic assumptions.
reflect: Why should an unexpected change be assessed in the context of time since surgery?

summary: IV therapy places a device within the vascular system, creating both a treatment route and potential complications.
body: Infiltration is leakage of nonvesicant fluid into tissue; extravasation involves a tissue-damaging vesicant. Phlebitis is vein inflammation. Access selection considers treatment, duration and vessels. Assessment includes the insertion site and infusion system: local symptoms can have several causes, and central venous access also carries systemic risks such as air embolism when air enters the circulation.
reflect: How might the same symptom require assessment for different IV complications?

summary: Raynaud phenomenon involves episodes of reduced blood flow to digits, often triggered by cold or emotional stress.
body: Temporary vessel narrowing produces color, temperature and sensation changes. Assessment distinguishes reversible episodes from tissue injury and considers whether another condition is contributing.

summary: Reduced arterial flow can limit oxygen delivery to limb tissues, particularly during activity.
body: Atherosclerosis commonly underlies lower-limb PAD. Buerger disease is a distinct inflammatory, thrombotic disorder strongly linked to tobacco exposure. Pain with activity, skin changes, pulses and tissue injury help characterize perfusion; some people with PAD have atypical symptoms or no reported symptoms.
reflect: Why might exertion reveal a circulation limitation before symptoms appear at rest?

summary: H1 antihistamines reduce selected histamine-mediated allergy symptoms.
body: First-generation H1 antihistamines commonly cause sedation and anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth. Second-generation agents are usually less sedating, but drowsiness can still occur and varies by drug and dose. Age, other sedatives and existing conditions affect tolerability and safety.

summary: Decongestants and intranasal corticosteroids act through different mechanisms.
body: Topical decongestants reduce nasal swelling through vasoconstriction; prolonged use can cause rebound congestion. Intranasal corticosteroids reduce inflammation and usually need consistent use, with fuller benefit developing over days to weeks. Technique, product instructions and the individual care plan guide expectations and duration.
reflect: Why should medicines with different mechanisms not be expected to work identically?

summary: Allergic responses vary from localized symptoms to potentially life-threatening systemic reactions.
body: Localized allergic inflammation differs from anaphylaxis, which can rapidly compromise airway, breathing or circulation, sometimes without skin findings. Emergency management of anaphylaxis centers on prompt intramuscular epinephrine under the applicable protocol. Antihistamines or topical anti-inflammatory medicines do not replace this treatment.
reflect: How does a systemic reaction differ from inflammation limited to the skin?
